description: ODC (EDIT and REFACTORING of a Setting): touch a Setting that THIS job did not create. The base is job:security-settings, that is, the two Settings, the server action that reads them and the screen already exist when the first op runs - there is not a single create here on purpose, because creating and editing in the same job proves no maintenance. MIND THE NAME: in the ODC product this is called Setting, but the public API kept OutSystems.Model.Data.ISiteProperty (and IESpace.CreateSiteProperty), so the targets say ISiteProperty and the vocabulary says Setting; in expressions the prefix is Settings.<name>. Outside the job that created them there are no aliases: the Settings are cited as 'ISiteProperty:Name' and the action as 'IServerAction:Name'. The target is the inherited WfCovMaxRows: its DefaultValue is switched (100 -> 250), its Description is rewritten over the other author's text, it is renamed to WfCovRowLimit and the TWO inherited expressions that read it are read back. The central proof is in the Raise message, where the SAME expression has both halves: the read Settings.<name>, which the platform rewrites by itself, and a text literal that cites the same name and does NOT follow. The second Setting, the secret WfCovAuditToken, answers what IsSecret changes: in the model, nothing - the DefaultValue is written and read the same, with no Verify complaining. What IsSecret changes is through WHICH path the write goes in, and that decides whether the data contract watches it (see the _why of (5a) and (8a)). The 55 Verify messages are the fixture's pre-existing ones.

ops.name: WfCovMaxRows
ops._why: (0) starting point: the Setting ALREADY exists before the first op of this job. It comes from the base job:security-settings, not from a create here. It returns a single ISiteProperty

(1) BEFORE, the inherited Setting: DataType Integer, DefaultValue 100, IsSecret False, IsMultiTenant Inherited, the Description written by the other job, and Referrers 2 - the two points of the inherited logic that read it. Compare with (5b), (6b) and (7b)

(2) BEFORE, the inherited SECRET Setting: IsSecret True, Referrers 1 and DefaultValue NULL - not because it is secret, but because nobody wrote it. It is this difference that makes the write of (8a) go in through a different door than that of (5a)

(3) BEFORE, who reads the Setting: count 2, real 2, both ITextBasedExpression, both inside WfCovAudit_Check - the condition of the If and the message of the Raise. They are REAL, inherited consumers; that is why the rename later is worth anything

(4) BEFORE, the text: 'Rows > Settings.WfCovMaxRows' in the If, and in the Raise '"Too many rows requested: the WfCovMaxRows setting allows " + IntegerToText(Settings.WfCovMaxRows)'. Note that this second expression says the name TWICE, once inside the literal and once in the read. This is the snapshot the dump (7c) is compared with

(5a) CHANGE 1 - the DefaultValue of an INHERITED Setting. The target is not a $alias: aliases are local to the job that declares them, and the one who declared this Setting was another job. The result says via 'expression.Text': ISiteProperty.DefaultValue is read-only and returns an IExpression, and since this Setting WAS BORN with a value the expression object already exists, so the kernel writes its Text instead of calling SetDefaultValue. That path does not enter the data contract (see (8a)), so here what proves it is the following get, not the contract
(5b) AFTER: DefaultValue 100 -> 250. DataType, IsSecret False and Referrers 2 STAYED - switching the default value touches no consumer

ops.value: Limite de linhas da auditoria. Description REESCRITA por setting-lifecycle.json, por cima do texto do job que criou a Setting. Cita WfCovMaxRows de proposito.
ops._why: (6a) CHANGE 2 - a Description that ALREADY had author text. There is a real REPLACEMENT, and not the filling of an empty field, which would prove much less. This is a normal property (via 'property'), so it is the one that shows up in the data contract. The old name stays in the text on purpose, so that the get (7b) shows that author text does not follow a rename
(6b) AFTER: the Description changed and the DefaultValue 250 of change 1 stayed. The two edits add up on the same Setting, they do not replace each other

ops.name: WfCovRowLimit
ops._why: (7a) CHANGE 3 - rename the inherited Setting WITH the real consumers linked. Rename is not creation, so it follows the convention of what already exists (the inherited name already carried the Wf prefix of the lane). It returns consumers=2 and expressionsRewritten=2: in the ODC lane the platform rewrites by itself the expressions that read the Setting

(7b) AFTER: the Name is different, the Key is the SAME and the Referrers are still 2. The Description still says WfCovMaxRows, a name that no longer exists in the module: Description is author text and no rename touches it. Only a hand corrects it - and this job leaves it like that on purpose, so the difference stays visible

(7c) READ BACK, THE CENTRAL PROOF: compare with the dump (4). The If already says 'Rows > Settings.WfCovRowLimit' without a single hand correction. And in the Raise the SAME expression ended up split in half: '"Too many rows requested: the WfCovMaxRows setting allows " + IntegerToText(Settings.WfCovRowLimit)' - the READ followed because it is a link by key, the LITERAL kept the old name because it is text. One expression, the two behaviours: it is the same thing that refactor-inherited.json shows for the name of a node, but here inside a single piece of text

(7d) the SAME two consumers, by the same keys as in the usages (3): w44YfZ7q...#Message and oWAaqeqp...#Condition. The rename changed the name and the text of the expressions; it neither created nor broke any link

ops.name: WfCovMaxRows
ops._why: (7e) empty list: the inherited name disappeared from the module, and from here on 'ISiteProperty:WfCovMaxRows' no longer resolves - that is why the following ops cite the new name

(8a) CHANGE 4, WHAT IsSecret CHANGES. The model accepts it: the result says via 'SetDefaultValue', the Model API call, because this Setting was born WITHOUT a value expression and so there is no Text to write. Two measured consequences. First: it is the only one of the two DefaultValue writes of this job that enters the data contract, because the 'expression.Text' path of (5a) only records assertions for DATA types and a Setting is not one. Second, and the one that matters to whoever writes Settings: neither the Verify nor the Model API prevents saving a default value on a secret Setting - what keeps the secret is the ODC Portal, not the Studio. The literal is chosen so that, if this is ever delivered, nobody mistakes it for a real secret

(8b) AFTER: the secret Setting returns the DefaultValue that was written to it, IsSecret is still True and the Referrers are still 1. This is what I want to be seen: the value stayed in plain text in the model and nothing complained
(9a) CHANGE 5 - the counter-proof: turn on IsSecret on a Setting that ALREADY has a DefaultValue. If the secret were policed by the model, this is where the value would be dropped
(9b) AFTER: IsSecret True and DefaultValue 250 INTACT. The flag is orthogonal to the value: it does not erase it, does not block it and does not give rise to any message in the Verify
(9c) restore the inherited state. This is the IsSecret write that the data contract checks at the end, because the assertion is by key and property: the second write replaces the first
(9d) AFTER: IsSecret False again, DefaultValue still 250. Going and coming back left no mark

(10) THE FINAL STATE of the edited Setting: new name, DefaultValue 250, Description rewritten (still citing the old name), IsSecret False, Referrers 2. All of this on top of an object that this job did not create

(11) the final state of the inherited logic, to put next to the dump (4): two expressions rewritten by the platform, zero hand corrections inside the flow, and a text literal that still says the old name, waiting for an author
